newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Workplace Relations deal a flash in the pan.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Workplace Relations deal a flash in the pan.

text.p: The government's deal with the Democrats on the Workplace Relations bill does not mean anything has changed in the Senate.

Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith said on Sunday: "It does reflect well on the Australian Democrats that they have been prepared to acknowledge the general thrust and direction of what we are trying to do and, rather than obstruct, to come to an agreement."

He has uttered a few similar warm fuzzies about the Democrats on Monday. Considering the thunderous message from voters at the Linday by-election, one might suppose that peace and love has descended on the upper house.

It is true that newly independent senator Mal Colston has changed Senate dynamics -- the Democrats now need to be a little more co-operative to do the deals with the government that they need to maintain their flow of publicity.
But the Workplace Relations deal is not a symptom of the new configuration of the Senate.
No one else, including Colston, would supply the two votes that the government needed to pass the bill, so this one was always going to be a Democrat deal.
Also, the Democrats have always backed small business. They may be a leftist party, but they are not strong union backers. Moderate industrial reform is perhaps their only right-wing policy.
They still do not believe in selling a third of Telstra and they remain opposed to big chunks of the budget.
It is possible that they may be moved by the by-election, but there is no sign of it yet.
OPPOSITION PICKS UP LABOUR MARKET ISSUE
Canberra Watch noted three weeks ago that the labour market was already slipping away from the government's forecasts.
A sharp rise in the rate of job creation will be needed if the economy is to meet the budget forecast of a 1.5 percent year-average employment growth in 1996/97.
Opposition treasury spokesman Gareth Evans confronted Treasurer Peter Costello with this on Monday (The context was the Workplace Relations bill and the government's promises of more jobs to come.)
Costello's noteworthy response was that the government was standing by the budget forecasts for economic growth, jobs and unemployment.
It will be worth watching Costello for the first time he declines to stand by the forecasts.
